role: Personal servant of the Prophet ﷺ for ten years
Most prolific hadith narrator among all the companions
Last surviving senior companion in Basrah
summary: Anas ibn Malik (RA) served as the personal attendant of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for the entirety of the Madinan period — ten years — beginning when he was approximately ten years old. He became the most prolific narrator of hadith among all the companions, with over 2,200 authenticated narrations. He lived to approximately 99-103 years, dying in Basrah in 93 AH, making him among the very last surviving companions of the Prophet ﷺ.
biography:
Anas ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr al-Khazraji al-Ansari was born in Madinah around 612 CE, from the tribe of Banu Khazraj, one of the two main Ansar tribes. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah upon the Hijrah in 1 AH, Anas was approximately ten years old. His mother Umm Sulaym bint Milhan (RA) — herself a distinguished companion — brought him to the Prophet ﷺ and offered him as a personal servant, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, every man from the Ansar has brought you a gift; I have nothing to offer except this son of mine — take him to serve you.' (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. 7; al-Dhahabi, Siyar A'lam al-Nubala', Vol. 3). The Prophet ﷺ accepted and Anas remained in his service for ten continuous years until the Prophet's death in 11 AH.

The relationship between Anas and the Prophet ﷺ was one of deep affection on both sides. Anas narrated: 'The Prophet ﷺ never said to me about anything I had done, "Why did you do that?" and never said about anything I had not done, "Why did you not do that?"' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Adab). This description of the Prophet's gentleness with his young servant became one of the foundational accounts of the Prophet's character. The Prophet ﷺ made du'a for Anas, saying: 'O Allah, give him wealth and children and bless him in them.' Anas later narrated that he had indeed been blessed with abundant wealth and many children and grandchildren, and that by the end of his life he had buried over eighty of his children. (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Manaqib)

As a child-servant in the Prophet's household during all ten years of the Madinan period, Anas had unparalleled access to the Prophet's daily life, habits, worship, and personal conduct. He witnessed things that other companions, even senior ones, never had the opportunity to observe. This proximity made him an irreplaceable source of hadith. He narrated what the Prophet wore, how he slept, what he ate, how he performed wudu, his physical appearance, his manner of greeting children, his expressions of affection, and countless other personal details that together constitute the most intimate portrait of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith literature.

Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' (Vol. 3) that Anas ibn Malik is the most prolific narrator of hadith among all the companions, with approximately 2,286 narrations attributed to him in the major hadith collections — surpassing even Abu Hurayrah (RA) according to some counts, though scholars differ on the exact tallies. This remarkable output is a direct consequence of his decade of daily proximity to the Prophet ﷺ.

Anas participated in the major battles of the prophetic period including the Battle of Badr (though as a young boy in a support role), and the subsequent campaigns. After the Prophet's death, he settled briefly in Madinah and then moved to Basrah during the early Islamic conquests, where he served as a teacher and religious authority. He participated in the conquest of Persia and witnessed the expansion of the Muslim world.

His longevity was extraordinary. He outlived virtually every other companion of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Dhahabi records that when he died in Basrah in 93 AH, scholars traveled from across the Muslim world to receive hadith from him as one of the last living links to the prophetic era. He was approximately 99 to 103 years old at his death — narrations differ on his exact birth year. His students in Basrah became the teachers of the next generation, including al-Hasan al-Basri who received narrations from Anas directly.

The Prophet ﷺ referred to Anas as 'my son' — a term of endearment — and the three du'as he made for Anas (for wealth, children, and blessing in them, as well as a specific du'a for the lengthening of his life) are all recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. All three are considered by scholars to have been visibly fulfilled in his life. Anas himself said near the end of his life: 'I am the last of those who directly served the Prophet ﷺ among the living.' (al-Dhahabi, Siyar, Vol. 3)

Ibn Sa'd, al-Dhahabi, al-Bukhari, and Muslim all treat the narrations of Anas with the highest level of authentication. He is one of the seven companions known as the Mukthirun (the prolific ones) who transmitted the largest numbers of hadith. His physical descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ — his face like the full moon, his hair, his walk, his smile — remain among the most vivid and cited in the entire seerah and shama'il literature.
